findings.pdf_says: Table 1 - COBOL character repertoire (Continued) | Basic special characters | - | minus sign (hyphen) |  -- the glyph printed in the Character column is the hyphen-minus (U+002D), the same width as the crossbar of the '+' glyph printed directly above it, and the Meaning column names it '(hyphen)'.
findings.markdown_says: | | – | minus sign (hyphen) |   (specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 5111; the Character cell holds U+2013 EN DASH, confirmed by codepoint dump)
findings.why_it_matters: Table 1 is the normative enumeration of the COBOL character repertoire - it is the definitive list of which characters a conforming implementation must accept in source. Transcribing the basic special character as U+2013 EN DASH puts a character that is NOT in the repertoire into the normative list and drops the one that is. Anything derived mechanically from this table (a lexer character class, a reserved-symbol table, a repertoire conformance test) would accept EN DASH as the minus/hyphen and reject the actual hyphen-minus, which is also the hyphen permitted inside COBOL words per 8.3.2.1. The Meaning column's own words '(hyphen)' contradict the transcribed character, so the markdown is internally inconsistent as well.
findings.suggested_repair: Replace the U+2013 EN DASH in the Character cell of the 'minus sign (hyphen)' row of Table 1 (specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 5111) with an ASCII hyphen-minus '-' (U+002D). Sweep the rest of the file for U+2013/U+2014 appearing in Character/glyph positions of syntax tables and general formats, where the standard prints hyphen-minus.

findings.pdf_says: 8.1.3   COBOL character repertoire   (a level-3 subclause nested under 8.1 Character sets, which is nested under Clause 8 Language fundamentals)
findings.markdown_says: ## 8.1.3 COBOL character repertoire   -- emitted at markdown level 2, i.e. SHALLOWER than its own parent '### 8.1 Character sets' (line 4973) and at the same level as the clause heading '## 8 Language fundamentals' (line 4967).
findings.why_it_matters: The heading depth is inverted relative to the standard's own numbering, so any tool that builds a table of contents, a section index, or a spec-citation resolver from the markdown headings will place 8.1.3 as a peer of Clause 8 rather than as a child of 8.1. The same inversion repeats on the neighbouring pages of this batch: '## 8.1.3.2 General rules' (p.121, line 5131) sits at level 2 while its sibling '### 8.1.3.1 General' (p.120, line 5082) sits at level 3; '## 8.1.4 Alphabets' and '## 8.1.5 Collating sequences' (p.123, lines 5178/5183) sit at level 2 while their siblings 8.1.1/8.1.2 sit at level 3; and '## 8.2.2 Locale field names' (p.125, line 5256) sits at level 2 while its sibling '### 8.2.1 General' (p.124, line 5210) sits at level 3. The heading TEXT and numbering are all correct - only the markdown level is wrong - so this is navigational, not normative. It appears to be a document-wide transcription pattern rather than a defect unique to these pages; fixing it should be done as one mechanical sweep, not page by page.
findings.suggested_repair: Derive the markdown heading level mechanically from the dotted section number (depth = number of dot-separated components, offset by the clause base level) and re-emit every numbered heading in specs/ISO_COBOL.md from that rule, so 8 -> level 2, 8.1 -> level 3, 8.1.3 -> level 4, 8.1.3.2 -> level 5. Do NOT hand-edit only the instances listed here.
